title: Number of Recent Calls
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning all history every call versus a sliding-window queue that actively evicts stale entries.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Implement the RecentCounter class, which counts the number of recent requests within a certain time frame: ping(t) adds a new request at time t (milliseconds) and returns the number of requests that have happened in the inclusive range [t - 3000, t] (including this new request itself). It is guaranteed that every call to ping uses a STRICTLY LARGER value of t than the previous call.

blocks.caption: A queue of timestamps directly models "recent requests": new pings enqueue at the back, and stale ones (older than the 3000ms window) are evicted from the front

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of calls to ping(t), with strictly increasing t values"],["Output","For each ping, the count of requests within the last 3000 milliseconds"],["Goal","Answer each ping in efficient (amortized O(1)) time, rather than rescanning all history each time"],["Constraints","1 <= t <= 10^9; each call to ping uses a t value strictly greater than the previous call's; at most 10^4 calls to ping"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Requests must be evicted once they fall OUTSIDE a sliding time window","A queue (FIFO), since the OLDEST requests are always the ones that expire first, exactly matching first-in-first-out order"],["Timestamps arrive in STRICTLY INCREASING order","This guarantees the queue naturally stays sorted, so evicting from the front (oldest first) is always correct without needing to search"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Every ping needs to know how many OTHER pings (including itself) fall within the last 3000 milliseconds; since pings arrive in increasing time order, the oldest pings are always the first ones to become too old and need removing.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Line at a Ticket Counter With a 3000ms "Recently Served" Window
blocks.text: Imagine tracking how many customers have been served in just the last few minutes at a busy counter, where customers are served strictly in the order they arrive. The OLDEST customer still being counted is always the first one to eventually fall outside the tracked window; removing them from the FRONT of a waiting line (a queue) as time passes is exactly the right structure for this.

blocks.caption: Each ping enqueues its timestamp, then the front of the queue is repeatedly dequeued while too old; the remaining queue size is the answer

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: ping(1), ping(100), ping(3001), ping(3002)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Queue after","Answer","Why"],"rows":[["ping(1)","[1]","1","The only ping so far, and 1 >= 1-3000"],["ping(100)","[1,100]","2","Both 1 and 100 are >= 100-3000=-2900"],["ping(3001)","[1,100,3001]","3","All three are >= 3001-3000=1 (1 is exactly at the boundary, inclusive)"],["ping(3002)","[100,3001,3002]","3","1 is now < 3002-3000=2, so it is evicted; the remaining 3 are all within range"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before rescanning the ENTIRE history of pings on every single call (wasteful, since most of that history was already confirmed to be recent or already evicted), notice that a queue directly and efficiently maintains "only the currently-recent pings" at all times.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since pings arrive in STRICTLY INCREASING time order, the queue (if maintained correctly) is always naturally sorted, with the OLDEST ping always at the front.

Observation 2: When a new ping arrives, only pings older than (t - 3000) need to be removed; since the queue is sorted, these are EXACTLY the ones sitting at the front, removable one at a time until the front is no longer too old.

Observation 3: After evicting every stale ping from the front, whatever REMAINS in the queue is, by definition, exactly the set of pings within the last 3000ms, so the queue's current SIZE directly answers the question.

Observation 4: Each ping is added to the queue exactly once, and removed from the queue at most once (whenever it eventually becomes stale), meaning the TOTAL work across all calls is bounded, even though a single call MIGHT evict many old pings at once.
This is a sliding-window queue technique: enqueue each new ping, then evict stale pings from the front until only recent ones remain; the queue's size directly answers each call.
6. Brute Force Solution
Remember every ping timestamp ever seen, and for each new ping, rescan the ENTIRE history, counting how many fall within the last 3000ms.
Step by step algorithm

items: Store every ping timestamp in a list, in order.
For each new ping, scan the entire list, counting timestamps that are >= (t - 3000).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Storing every timestamp directly reflects "remember the full history," making the counting logic straightforward, if repetitive.
Rescanning the entire list every call directly implements the definition, but revisits already-confirmed-recent (or already-known-stale) entries unnecessarily.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly counts recent requests, since a full rescan always finds every timestamp within the required range.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per call in the worst case, O(n^2) total across n calls.
Space: O(n), for the growing list of all timestamps.
Limitation: rescanning ALL history on every call is wasteful, especially as old, already-stale timestamps accumulate; a queue that actively evicts stale entries keeps only what is actually needed.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force keeps EVERY timestamp forever, rescanning all of them each call. Instead, use a queue: enqueue each new ping, then repeatedly dequeue from the FRONT while it is older than (t - 3000). Since the queue naturally stays sorted (timestamps arrive in increasing order), this always correctly evicts exactly the stale entries, and the resulting queue size directly answers the question.
Maintain a queue (deque). On ping(t): enqueue t at the back; while the front of the queue is < t - 3000, dequeue it; return the queue's current size.
9. Optimized Solution
Enqueue each new ping, evict stale entries from the front, and return the queue's size directly.
Dry run for ping(1), ping(100), ping(3001), ping(3002)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The sequence of answers is [1,2,3,3], matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) amortized per call: each timestamp is enqueued exactly once and dequeued at most once across the entire sequence of calls.
Space: O(n), for the queue in the worst case (if the 3000ms window never evicts much).
Why This Works

Since timestamps arrive in strictly increasing order, the queue is ALWAYS sorted from oldest (front) to newest (back). This guarantees that the FIRST entries to become stale are always exactly the ones at the front, so a simple "evict from the front while too old" loop always removes exactly the right entries, never leaving a stale one behind or removing a still-valid one.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A new ping arrives","Enqueued at the back, becoming the newest entry"],["The front of the queue is older than t - 3000","Dequeued (evicted), repeating until the front is recent enough"],["The queue's final state after eviction","Contains exactly the pings within the last 3000ms; its size is the direct answer"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: A deque (double-ended queue) is used specifically because it supports O(1) removal from the FRONT, unlike a plain array/list which would need O(n) shifting.
The while loop (not a single if) correctly handles evicting MULTIPLE stale entries at once, if a large time gap has passed since the last ping.
Returning the queue's size directly, with no separate counting loop, is what achieves the O(1) amortized answer time.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (rescan all history every call)","O(n) per call, O(n^2) total","O(n)","Keeps every timestamp forever, rescanning unnecessarily"],["Optimized (sliding-window queue)","O(1) amortized per call, O(n) total","O(n)","Actively evicts stale entries, keeping only what is currently needed"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

A "count/track items within a sliding time (or value) window" problem, where items arrive in sorted order, is a natural fit for a queue: the oldest items are always the first to expire, and a queue's FIFO structure directly and efficiently manages this.
Common mistakes

items: Using a plain array/list instead of a proper queue/deque, incurring O(n) cost for removing from the front instead of O(1).
Using a single if instead of a while loop for eviction, which would fail to remove MULTIPLE stale entries when a large time gap occurs.
Miscounting the boundary condition: the window is INCLUSIVE, so a timestamp exactly equal to (t - 3000) should still count.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["The very first ping","The queue starts empty, so after enqueuing, the answer is simply 1"],["Pings spaced far more than 3000ms apart","Each ping evicts ALL previous entries, so the answer resets to 1 each time"],["Many pings arriving within a very short time span","None get evicted, so the answer grows steadily with each call"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating "the guarantee that t is strictly increasing is what makes the queue ALWAYS sorted, and thus evicting from the front always correct" demonstrates understanding of exactly why a queue (not some other structure) is the right fit here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count/track items within a SLIDING time window," with items arriving in order, points directly to a queue: oldest items are evicted from the front as they expire.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: What if timestamps could arrive OUT of order (not strictly increasing)? A queue alone would no longer suffice, since eviction could not simply happen from the front; a different structure (like a balanced BST or sorted structure) would be needed to efficiently find and remove arbitrary stale entries.
How would you adapt this to a DIFFERENT window size, configurable at runtime? The exact same technique applies directly; only the fixed "3000" constant would become a parameter.
What is the worst-case space usage, and when does it occur? O(n), occurring when pings arrive frequently enough that few (or none) ever get evicted before the next one arrives.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The foundational "sliding window via a queue" pattern, related to Moving Average from Data Stream and Design Hit Counter elsewhere in this category, all relying on the same FIFO-eviction idea for time- or size-bounded windows.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) per call, O(n^2) total; O(n) space.
Optimized (sliding-window queue): O(1) amortized per call; O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sliding-window queue (FIFO eviction)

Core Idea: Enqueue each new ping; since timestamps arrive sorted, evicting stale entries from the FRONT (via a while loop) always correctly maintains exactly the recent window; the queue's size is the direct answer
Time: O(1) amortized per call
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: The guarantee of strictly increasing timestamps is what makes front-eviction always correct, without ever needing to search the queue
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Enqueue t; while front < t-3000, dequeue; return queue size
